passage:
Ujjwal called the all-night gaming stress relief. Two lectures missed, a card statement he kept folded in a drawer, and still he told his roommate, "I can stop anytime." Then the sun would come up on another round.

His mother Jaya found the college notice and the statement together, and she shouted. "Are you throwing your life away?" Ujjwal felt cornered, and his first thought was to say it was nothing and shut his door. Then he saw her hands shaking. "You're scared," he said. "I am," she said, and sat down. By the end of the evening they had agreed he would book an appointment.

In the clinic his palms were damp. He nearly described only the mild half, a few late nights, then said, "It's more than that. I play till morning and I skip things." The doctor listened and set a follow-up. The next week he slipped and went back anyway.

A month later he sat on a plastic chair in a community hall. Bhavna, who ran the circle, smiled at him. "Nobody here will judge you. Just say what's true." He said it, and something in his chest let go. The following week he came again.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal tell his roommate about his gaming?
qa.a: He said, "I can stop anytime."

qa.q: How did Ujjwal's reaction to his mother's shouting differ from the way he talked at the clinic and at the circle?
qa.a: With Jaya he first felt cornered and wanted to shut himself away, until he saw she was scared. At the clinic and the circle he told the whole truth, and he kept going after a slip, which is how the plan began to work.

qa.q: What was Ujjwal feeling when Bhavna said nobody would judge him?
qa.a: He felt relief and a sense of belonging, shown by the way something in his chest let go.

qa.q: What could Ujjwal do if he slips again after weeks of going to the circle?
qa.a: He could go back to the doctor and the circle honestly, as he did after his first slip, and tell someone safe what happened.

grounding: One young adult's gaming habit is met by his own denial, a parent's fearful anger, a doctor's appointment and a group that accepts him.

passage:
In the corridor Mehak grinned at the poster of the leader Jagdish supported and said, "Your hero is a joke." His face burned and he almost shot back an insult. Instead he breathed and asked, "What do you mean by that?" Mehak shrugged and said her father's shop had shut after a new rule. It was not what Jagdish wanted to hear, but it was a reason.

That weekend at dinner his uncle Sohan jabbed a fork at him. "Your lot only repeat slogans." Jagdish's voice climbed to match, until he heard the worry underneath, about Sohan's pension. He said, more quietly, "Can I show you what I read?" When Sohan grew loud again, Jagdish said, "Let's finish this another day, uncle," and left the table politely.

Later, scrolling, he caught himself thinking that everyone on the other side was stupid. It felt good, and there was nobody to tell. On Monday Vidya, who backed the rival party, lent him a pencil, and he asked her why she believed what she did. Her answer was about her mother's clinic, ordinary and thoughtful.

When strangers online called him names over his view and his faith, he did not reply. He blocked them, saved screenshots and showed his teacher. That same day the teacher reported it to the school office.

qa.q: Whose father's shop had shut after a new rule?
qa.a: Mehak's father's shop had shut after a new rule.

qa.q: How did Jagdish's handling of Mehak's mockery differ from his handling of the strangers online?
qa.a: With Mehak he paused and asked what she meant, which let him hear a reason. With the strangers, who were only cruel, he did not reply, but blocked them, saved proof and told his teacher.

qa.q: What was Jagdish feeling when he was sure everyone on the other side was stupid?
qa.a: It felt good to him, but it also left him lonely, since he had nobody to tell.

qa.q: What could Jagdish do next time his uncle gets loud at dinner?
qa.a: He could listen for the worry underneath, keep his facts calm, and leave politely if it gets heated, since the relationship matters more than winning.

grounding: One teen meets political disagreement through anger, a family clash, growing contempt and online abuse, and each is handled differently.

passage:
The day after Nana's funeral Nazia went to school and felt nothing at all, like a coat hung on a hook. Then in maths, the smell of cardamom tea from a classmate's flask made her cry so hard the teacher let her step into the corridor. That evening she sat with the family for prayers, and let her aunt's arm stay round her shoulders.

What she could not shake was the last phone call: she had hung up on Nana after a quarrel about screen time. The thought looped every night. She finally wrote him a letter. "Nana, I am sorry for my tone. I meant to tell you your stories were my favourite thing." Some nights she was furious, and once she said it aloud in the prayer room, "Why him?" Her mother did not shush her. She only said, "Say it. It's allowed."

At school Anand and Darshan talked about cricket scores and nobody mentioned Nana. It stung, until Nazia told Anand at lunch, "Please don't act like it didn't happen. Just ask how I am, or sit with me." Anand went red. "I didn't know what to say." Next day he sat beside her with two rotis, and Darshan brought a small card.

qa.q: What smell made Nazia cry in maths class?
qa.a: The smell of cardamom tea from a classmate's flask made her cry.

qa.q: How did Nazia's guilt about the last phone call and her anger in the prayer room differ, and how did each get voiced?
qa.a: The guilt was about hanging up on Nana after a quarrel, and she voiced it in a letter of apology. The anger was aimed at whoever let Nana die, and she said it aloud in the prayer room while her mother let her.

qa.q: What was Nazia feeling when Anand and Darshan talked about cricket and said nothing about Nana?
qa.a: She felt hurt and alone, because it stung to have her loss ignored.

qa.q: How could a friend like Anand support Nazia in the days after the funeral?
qa.a: He could ask how she is, sit with her at lunch and bring something small, as he did, instead of staying silent.

grounding: After a grandfather's death a teen moves through numbness, sudden tears, guilt, anger and classmates' silence within one family loss.

passage:
Three children were building a train track in the block corner. Minakshi held the red engine tightly and told Saurabh, "You can't play." His lip shook and his eyes stung, and he walked to the window. Beside the tunnel, Jaya had her own small blue truck, and Minakshi grabbed it too. Jaya froze. Her face crumpled, she let go and hid behind the shelf, crying without a sound.

The teacher had been watching from across the room, and came over calmly. "I saw the train and the truck. Minakshi, tell me what happened. Jaya, you too. Saurabh, would you like to tell me?" Saurabh said in a small voice, "I felt sad because I was told I can't play." The teacher listened to all three, set a sand timer on the shelf and said, "Turns." Nobody was told they were bad.

Next day Minakshi reached for Jaya's truck again. This time Jaya said, "Stop!" as loudly as she could and called, "Teacher!" Minakshi's hand dropped.

At tidy-up time Saurabh was still a little cross, but he missed the trains. He walked over and said, "Okay, let's play again," and held out the green carriage for Minakshi to take a turn.

qa.q: What did the teacher put on the shelf to set turns?
qa.a: The teacher put a sand timer on the shelf.

qa.q: How did Jaya's reaction the first time Minakshi grabbed her truck differ from her reaction the next day, and what did the teacher add?
qa.a: The first time Jaya froze, cried and gave up the truck, hiding. The next day she said stop loudly and called the teacher. In between, the teacher listened to everyone and set turns with a timer, which showed her that adults can help.

qa.q: What was Saurabh feeling when he walked to the window?
qa.a: He felt sad and left out after being told he could not play.

qa.q: What could Saurabh do if he is still cross and Minakshi grabs again?
qa.a: He could say stop loudly and tell the teacher, and he can be a little cross while still choosing, when ready, to offer a turn.

grounding: A toy dispute in the block corner shows exclusion, a frozen child who later says stop, a teacher's fair turns, and a child who chooses to make up.

passage:
After his last exam Omkar sat at home for three weeks and called himself lazy and lost. "You've wasted everything," he told the ceiling. At Yash's rooftop party Yash talked about his job offer and a plan for a masters, and Omkar smiled while his stomach sank. Scrolling in bed, he found ten more friends with neat futures and felt behind.

Then he bumped into Baljeet, a neighbour who ran a ceramics workshop. He asked how she had found her way. She laughed. "I changed course three times. I was an accountant, then a teacher, then this. I didn't know until I was doing it." Omkar walked home thinking about that. She also said, "If the heaviness doesn't lift, talk to a counsellor. That isn't weakness."

One evening his grandmother handed him an old copy of a spiritual text she read each night. He read a few pages, found some of it comforting and some of it hard to accept, and joined a small reading group at the library to argue about it. He did not take every line as the answer.

The next morning he took one small step: he signed up for a Saturday pottery class.

qa.q: What did Baljeet do for a living?
qa.a: Baljeet ran a ceramics workshop.

qa.q: How did Omkar's talk with Baljeet and his comparison with Yash lead him in different directions?
qa.a: Watching Yash's neat plans made Omkar feel behind, while Baljeet's story of changing course three times showed him that direction forms while doing things. That made him try a small step, the pottery class.

qa.q: What was Omkar feeling when he called himself lazy and lost?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and hopeless about his life, believing his youth was wasted.

qa.q: What could Omkar do if the heavy feeling does not lift even after the pottery class?
qa.a: He could talk to a counsellor, as Baljeet said, and be kind to himself while taking another tiny step.

grounding: One young adult's lost purpose shows harsh self-labels, envy of friends, a mentor's winding story and a text read with others.

passage:
At the agency's office, Yusuf slid a folder across the table. "Sign today or the rate goes up." Divyansh noticed that the payment date they had promised out loud was missing from the pages, and there was a fee he had not heard of. "Please put both in writing," he said. Yusuf refused, and Divyansh picked up his bag and left.

It was an older mistake that still stung. Months earlier he had signed a co-working agreement without reading it properly, and now the exit terms were tighter than he remembered. He felt foolish. He took it to Minakshi, a lawyer, who went through the clauses. "In plain words, this one means you pay for the whole year if you leave early." She explained the risks, then added, "It's your decision. I can tell you what I see." Together they drafted a request to amend the agreement.

The co-working owner's reply came within the hour, and it was hot. He was accused of breaking the terms and threatened with legal action. Divyansh took a breath, reread the agreement, gathered the emails and wrote a calm reply that stuck to dates and clauses. At the end he suggested a mediator. He did not answer the last angry call.

qa.q: What was missing from the pages Yusuf pushed Divyansh to sign?
qa.a: The payment date promised out loud was missing, and there was a fee he had not heard of.

qa.q: How did Divyansh's approach with Yusuf's rushed folder differ from the way he dealt with the co-working agreement?
qa.a: With Yusuf he insisted the terms be in writing and walked away when refused. With the co-working agreement he had already signed without reading, so he brought it to Minakshi and then asked to amend it in writing.

qa.q: What was Divyansh feeling when he realised the exit terms were tighter than he remembered?
qa.a: He felt foolish and regretful, as he had signed without reading properly.

qa.q: What could Divyansh do if the co-working owner keeps threatening action?
qa.a: He could keep replies calm and in writing, keep his emails and proofs, and ask Minakshi or a mediator for help before it escalates.

grounding: One professional faces a pushy deal, an old unfavourable signature, a lawyer's plain-language help and an angry counterparty in the same contract story.
